elements.text: Give urgent attention to the patient with constipation and:

elements.section: Give urgent attention to the patient with constipation and:
elements.text: No stools or flatus/wind in the past 24 hours with abdominal pain/distension

Approach to the patient with constipation not needing urgent attention • Review diet, fluid intake and medication (amitriptyline, schizophrenia treatment, codeine and morphine can cause constipation: discuss with doctor). • Advise that regular use of enemas or laxatives can worsen constipation. • If pregnant, give routine antenatal care 175. Advise that constipation is common during pregnancy and give advice as below. • Check Hb. If < 12 (woman) or < 13(man), anaemia likely 44. • If weakness/tiredness, weight gain, low mood, dry skin or cold intolerance, check TSH. If abnormal, refer to doctor. • If patient is bed-bound or has a life-limiting illness, also give palliative care 191. • If > 65 years, bed-bound/receiving palliative care, or overflow diarrhoea (prolonged constipation followed by watery stool), check for solid immobile bulk of stool in rectum. If present, impaction likely: refer.
Advise the patient with constipation on behavioural changes • Advise that certain behavioural changes can help reduce the risk of colorectal cancer:

Encourage patient at least 30 minutes of brisk physical activity (such as walking) at least 5 days a week. Increase activities of daily living like gardening, housework, walking instead of taking transport, using stairs instead of lifts.
If patient drinks alcohol, advise to stop 165.
Advise a high fibre diet (vegetables, fruit, coarse mielie meal, bran and cooked dried prunes), with adequate fluid intake.
If patient smokes, encourage to stop 164.

Treat the patient with constipation • If no better with diet and exercise, give sennosides A and B 13.5mg at night or lactulose 10-20 mL once daily. If needed, increase sennosides A and B to 2 tablets (up to 4 tablets at night), or increase lactulose to 12 hourly. • If any of: > 65 years old/frail, postpartum woman, spinal disease, severe cognitive impairment, pelvic organ/rectal prolapse after surgery, refer to rehabilitation services for bowel care. • If no response after 1 week of laxative use, or if recent change in bowel habits, weight loss, blood in stool or occult blood positive, or cause uncertain, refer.

Assess the patient with constipation for colorectal cancer • Patient has an increased risk of colorectal cancer if > 50 years old and any of: - Previous history of colorectal cancer, polyps, ulcerative colitis, or Crohn's disease - Family history of colorectal cancer in first-degree relative (parent, sibling or child), especially if diagnosed before age 60, or family history of multiple polyps or Lynch syndrome. • Ask about common colorectal cancer symptoms: - Change in bowel habits like constipation, diarrhoea, or change in stool consistency - Rectal bleeding or visible blood in stool - Persistent abdominal discomfort including cramps, gas or pain - A feeling that the bowel does not empty completely after defecation (tenesmus) - Unexplained weight loss/weakness/fatigue. • If patient has any of above symptoms, discuss/refer.
